title: Implement Magic Dictionary
statement:
Build a class `MagicDictionary` that holds a set of distinct words and answers whether a query word becomes one of them after replacing exactly one of its letters with a different letter.

- `MagicDictionary()` creates the structure with no words.
- `buildDict(dictionary)` stores the words of `dictionary`, which are all different. It is called exactly once, before any `search`.
- `search(searchWord)` returns `true` when some stored word has the same length as `searchWord` and differs from it in exactly one position, and `false` otherwise. A stored word equal to `searchWord` does not count, because one letter must actually change; letters cannot be inserted or deleted.
constraints: dictionary[i] contains only lowercase English letters
The words in dictionary are distinct
searchWord contains only lowercase English letters
buildDict is called once, before any search
At most 100 calls are made to search
notes:
## Intuition

The direct check compares `searchWord` against every stored word of the same length and counts mismatched letters, which costs O(n · L) per query. A hash map can do better. Two equal-length words differ in exactly one position `i` precisely when they become identical after their letter at `i` is replaced by a wildcard `*`. So store every wildcard pattern of every word, and a query only needs to look up its own patterns. The one subtlety: the pattern also matches the query word itself, so the map counts how many stored words produce each pattern.

## Approach

1. Keep `words`, the set of stored words, and `patterns`, a map from each wildcard pattern to how many stored words produce it.
2. `buildDict`: for each `word` and each position `i`, build `pattern` by putting `*` at `i`, and increase its count.
3. `search`: for each position `i` of `searchWord`, build the same kind of `pattern` and read its `count`.
4. If `count > 1`, at least one of those words is not `searchWord`, so it differs only at `i`: return `true`.
5. If `count === 1` and `searchWord` is not stored, the single matching word differs from it at `i`: return `true`.
6. If no position works, return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

`buildDict(["hello", "leetcode"])` stores five patterns for `hello` (`*ello`, `h*llo`, `he*lo`, `hel*o`, `hell*`) and eight for `leetcode`, each with count 1. `search("hello")`: every pattern has count 1, but `hello` itself is stored, so the only match is the word itself: `false`. `search("hhllo")`: `*hllo` is absent, then `h*llo` has count 1 and `hhllo` is not stored: `true`. `search("hell")` and `search("leetcoded")` have lengths 4 and 9, so none of their patterns exist: `false`, `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: `buildDict` is O(Σ L²) because each of a word's L patterns is a new string of length L; `search` is O(L²) for a query of length L.
- Space: O(Σ L²) for the stored patterns.

## Pitfalls

- An exact match is not enough: `search("hello")` with `hello` stored is `false` unless another stored word is one letter away.
- A count of 1 is ambiguous: check whether that single word is `searchWord` itself before answering `true`.
- Words of different lengths never match; inserting or deleting a letter is not allowed.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `words` | set of the stored words |
| `patterns` | map from a word with one letter replaced by `*` to how many stored words give it |
| `i` | the position being replaced by the wildcard |
| `pattern` | the current word with `*` at position `i` |
| `count` | how many stored words share the query's `pattern` |

narration.4: patterns counts, for each word with one letter blanked out, how many stored words give it.
